subject: Electrolytes
title: Calcium & Magnesium Diagnostic Pearls
preview: Interpret calcium and magnesium disorders using symptoms, ionized calcium and a careful review of albumin and medications.

sections.title: Check what the calcium test actually measures
points: Total calcium is affected by albumin, while ionized calcium reflects the biologically active fraction.
Albumin-corrected calcium formulas are imperfect, particularly in critical illness, and should not replace ionized measurement when decisions are consequential.

sections.title: Recognize the clinical contrasts
points: Hypocalcemia can cause neuromuscular excitability, muscle spasms and prolonged QT interval.
Hypercalcemia can cause polyuria, thirst, constipation, confusion and a shortened QT interval.

sections.title: Choose cause-directed assessment
points: Review renal function, phosphate, magnesium, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D in the appropriate clinical context.
Severe symptomatic abnormalities require an urgent, monitored treatment pathway.

sections.title: Exam trap: magnesium can be the missing link
points: Persistent hypocalcemia or hypokalemia despite replacement may reflect hypomagnesemia.
A single total calcium number without albumin and ionized context can be misleading.

quickRevision: When calcium results conflict with the clinical picture, check ionized calcium rather than relying only on albumin-adjusted totals.
Symptomatic hypocalcemia may cause perioral tingling, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation; hypercalcemia may cause dehydration and altered cognition.
Hypomagnesemia can impair parathyroid hormone action and make associated potassium or calcium abnormalities refractory.

quiz.question: Which electrolyte disturbance may occur with hypomagnesemia?
quiz.explanation: Refractory hypokalemia. Persistent hypocalcemia or hypokalemia despite replacement may reflect hypomagnesemia.
